Vignette:
# Clinical Vignette: Rajesh Patel

Rajesh Patel is a seventy-six-year-old South Asian electrician who presented for assessment six months after a mugging that left him shaken but physically unharmed. He arrived at the clinic with his wife, Meera, who had insisted he seek help after noticing changes in him that had accumulated over the preceding months—changes he himself had tried to minimize but could no longer ignore.

The mugging occurred on a Friday evening in late September as Rajesh walked home from a supply store near his neighborhood in Queens. He had been a self-employed electrician for nearly fifty years, accustomed to moving through the city with ease, and this particular errand was routine. Two men approached him from behind as he waited at a traffic light. One grabbed his shoulder hard enough that he stumbled; the other demanded his wallet while brandishing something Rajesh could not clearly see in the darkness. The encounter lasted perhaps ninety seconds. Rajesh handed over his wallet. The men ran. He was not struck, not cut, not physically injured beyond a bruise on his shoulder. But something in that moment—the sudden loss of control, the sense of being trapped between the curb and the street with nowhere to move, the smell of cheap whiskey on the breath of the man who grabbed him—had lodged itself in his nervous system in a way that would not release.

In the weeks that followed, Rajesh found himself unable to sleep through the night. He would wake in the small hours, his heart racing, sometimes drenched in sweat, always disoriented. These nightmares were vivid and fragmented—sometimes he was on that street corner again, sometimes the men were in his apartment, sometimes he was frozen and unable to call out. What troubled him most was the residue these dreams left behind. Even after he was fully awake, even after Meera reassured him that he was safe at home, the sense of dread would cling to him. He would lie in bed in the dark, unable to return to sleep, convinced that something terrible was about to happen. Daytime felt safer, but night had become a territory he could no longer fully trust.

As autumn turned to winter, Rajesh began to avoid situations he had previously navigated without thought. The subway, which he had used for decades, now felt impossible. Crowded places—the grocery store on Saturday mornings, the temple he and Meera attended—triggered a suffocating sense of exposure. He could not explain it clearly, but the presence of other bodies around him, the unpredictability of their movements, made him hypervigilant and exhausted. His hands would shake. He would feel an urge to leave, to get to open space, to put his back against a wall where he could see everyone approaching.

More troubling still was his response to strangers. A neighbor greeting him from across the street would set his jaw tight. A delivery person at the door would cause his pulse to quicken. He was aware that this reaction was disproportionate—he knew intellectually that these were ordinary people—but his body did not believe what his mind was trying to tell it. He had come to believe that strangers represented danger, that their approach was inherently threatening, that he could not predict what they might do.

The smell of alcohol became a particular torment. At a family gathering in December, a relative arrived with wine on his breath, and Rajesh found himself rigid, unable to continue the conversation, eventually excusing himself to the garage. He had not realized until that moment how completely the smell of whiskey—and now, increasingly, any alcohol—had become fused in his mind with the mugging. The scent alone could transport him back to that street corner, could trigger the same flood of adrenaline and fear.

By February, Rajesh had stopped taking electrical jobs that required him to travel by public transportation. He had begun to decline invitations from friends. Meera had noticed him checking the locks on their apartment door multiple times each evening, a habit that had not existed before. He spent his nights reading in the living room, unwilling to lie in bed in the dark, watching the windows, listening for sounds. The man who had built his reputation on reliability and steady competence was becoming isolated, and he knew it was unsustainable.

What finally brought him to the clinic was Meera's ultimatum, delivered gently but firmly: she loved him, but she could not watch him disappear into fear. Rajesh arrived uncertain whether therapy could help a man his age recover from something that felt, in the dark hours, like permanent damage to his sense of safety in the world. What he hoped for most was the return of his nights—the ability to sleep without vigilance, to trust the darkness as he once had.
